title: Immunology and Serology
description: Cells and organs of the immune system, antigen–antibody reactions, serological techniques, immunoassays, and serological diagnosis of infections and autoimmune diseases.

topics.title: Components of the Immune System
topics.summary: Innate and adaptive immunity, lymphoid organs, lymphocytes, MHC and cytokines.

notes.b: Primary lymphoid organs are the bone marrow (B-cell maturation) and thymus (T-cell maturation); secondary lymphoid organs (lymph nodes, spleen, MALT such as tonsils and Peyer's patches) are where immune responses are initiated. Innate immunity: physical barriers, phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages), natural killer cells, complement, dendritic cells, and pattern-recognition receptors (e.g. Toll-like receptors). Adaptive immunity: B lymphocytes (CD19, CD20; produce antibodies after differentiating into plasma cells) and T lymphocytes (CD3) — helper T cells (CD4; Th1 activate macrophages, Th2 help B cells and eosinophils, Th17, regulatory T cells) and cytotoxic T cells (CD8; kill virus-infected and tumour cells). Memory cells provide faster secondary responses.
k: Bone marrow and thymus: primary organs

notes.b: The major histocompatibility complex (human leucocyte antigens, HLA, on chromosome 6) presents antigens to T cells: MHC class I (HLA-A, B, C — on all nucleated cells) presents endogenous (e.g. viral) peptides to CD8 T cells; MHC class II (HLA-DR, DP, DQ — on antigen-presenting cells: dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells) presents exogenous peptides to CD4 T cells. HLA matching is important in transplantation; certain HLA types are associated with diseases (e.g. HLA-B27 with ankylosing spondylitis; HLA-B*5701 with abacavir hypersensitivity). Cytokines: IL-1, TNF-α and IL-6 (inflammation, fever), IL-2 (T-cell growth), IFN-γ (macrophage activation), IL-4 and IL-5 (allergy, eosinophils), IL-10 and TGF-β (regulatory).
k: MHC I → CD8; MHC II → CD4

topics.title: Antigen–Antibody Reactions
topics.summary: Immunoglobulin structure and classes, affinity and avidity, agglutination and precipitation.

notes.b: Antibodies (immunoglobulins) have two heavy and two light chains (κ or λ) forming Fab regions (antigen binding) and an Fc region (effector functions such as complement activation and binding to Fc receptors). Classes: IgG (most abundant, 4 subclasses, crosses the placenta, secondary response, opsonisation), IgM (pentamer, first in primary response, best complement activator and agglutinator), IgA (dimer in secretions — mucosal immunity, breast milk), IgE (mast cells — allergy and helminths), IgD (B-cell receptor). Affinity is the strength of a single antigen-binding site; avidity is the overall binding strength of a multivalent antibody. Antibody avidity increases with time after infection (useful for dating infections like toxoplasmosis, rubella).

Agglutination occurs when antibodies cross-link particulate antigens (cells, latex particles) — used in blood grouping, Widal test, rheumatoid factor latex test and ASO. Precipitation occurs with soluble antigens forming lattices (immunodiffusion — Ouchterlony double diffusion, radial immunodiffusion). The prozone phenomenon (antibody excess) can cause false-negative agglutination or flocculation tests (e.g. VDRL in secondary syphilis) — diluting the serum resolves it. Complement fixation tests, neutralisation tests and haemagglutination inhibition (influenza) are other classical methods. Titre is the highest dilution giving a positive reaction; a fourfold rise between acute and convalescent sera indicates recent infection.
k: Fourfold rise in titre = recent infection

topics.title: Immunoassays and Modern Techniques
topics.summary: ELISA, rapid diagnostic tests, immunofluorescence, flow cytometry and Western blot.

notes.b: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA) detect antigens or antibodies using enzyme-labelled reagents and a colour-producing substrate (e.g. horseradish peroxidase with TMB). Formats: indirect ELISA (detects antibody — e.g. HIV antibody), sandwich ELISA (detects antigen with capture and detection antibodies — e.g. HBsAg, p24), and competitive ELISA. Fourth-generation HIV tests detect both antibodies and p24 antigen, shortening the window period. Chemiluminescence immunoassays offer higher sensitivity and automation. Lateral-flow rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) use immunochromatography with a test line and a control line (which must appear for a valid result) — widely used for HIV, malaria, hepatitis B, syphilis and pregnancy. The high-dose hook effect can cause false negatives in sandwich immunoassays with extremely high antigen levels.

Immunofluorescence uses fluorochrome-labelled antibodies (direct or indirect) viewed under a fluorescence microscope — e.g. antinuclear antibody (ANA) testing on HEp-2 cells with pattern reporting. Flow cytometry analyses cells in suspension using fluorescent antibodies and lasers — used for CD4 counts in HIV, immunophenotyping of leukaemias and lymphomas, and PNH testing. Western blot separates proteins by electrophoresis and detects specific antibodies — once used to confirm HIV. Immunoturbidimetry and nephelometry measure proteins (CRP, immunoglobulins, complement C3/C4) by light scattering. Point-of-care CD4 analysers support HIV care in rural areas. All immunoassays require internal quality control and participation in external quality assessment.
k: IIF for ANA on HEp-2 cells

topics.title: Serological Diagnosis of Infections
topics.summary: HIV testing algorithms, hepatitis B and C markers, syphilis serology, and other serological tests.

notes.b: Nigeria's HIV testing uses a serial algorithm of rapid tests: a highly sensitive first test (screening); if reactive, a highly specific second test; discordant results use a third tie-breaker and retesting. The window period is the time after infection before tests become positive (shorter with fourth-generation assays); infants under 18 months need DNA/RNA PCR. HIV viral load monitors treatment. Hepatitis B markers: HBsAg (current infection; > 6 months = chronic), anti-HBs (immunity — after vaccination alone or recovery), anti-HBc (past or current infection — IgM anti-HBc indicates acute infection), HBeAg (high infectivity, replication), anti-HBe and HBV DNA. A vaccinated person is HBsAg-negative, anti-HBs-positive and anti-HBc-negative. Hepatitis C: anti-HCV screening followed by HCV RNA to confirm active infection.
k: Serial HIV algorithm: sensitive then specific

notes.b: Syphilis serology: non-treponemal tests (VDRL, RPR — detect antibodies to cardiolipin; titres reflect disease activity and fall with treatment; false positives in pregnancy, malaria, autoimmune disease, TB and old age) and treponemal tests (TPHA, TPPA, FTA-ABS, treponemal EIA, rapid treponemal tests — remain positive for life). Diagnosis usually requires both. Other serological tests: Widal test for typhoid (anti-O and anti-H agglutinins — poor specificity in endemic areas, overused in Nigeria; blood culture preferred), antistreptolysin O (ASO — recent streptococcal infection; rheumatic fever), rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP (rheumatoid arthritis), Brucella agglutination, and IgM/IgG serology for rubella, toxoplasma, CMV and dengue.

topics.title: Hypersensitivity, Autoimmunity and Transplant Immunology
topics.summary: Laboratory investigation of allergy, autoimmune diseases, complement and HLA typing.

notes.b: Allergy (type I hypersensitivity) is investigated by total and specific IgE measurements, skin prick testing (in clinics), and serum tryptase (raised after anaphylaxis — sample within about 1–3 hours). Autoimmune disease investigations: antinuclear antibodies (ANA — sensitive screen for SLE), anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith (specific for SLE), complement C3 and C4 (low in active SLE and immune-complex glomerulonephritis), rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP (rheumatoid arthritis — anti-CCP more specific), anti-TPO and TSH-receptor antibodies (autoimmune thyroid disease), anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA (coeliac disease), ANCA (vasculitis), anti-GBM (Goodpasture's syndrome), anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies (myasthenia gravis) and islet autoantibodies (anti-GAD — type 1 diabetes).
k: ANA: sensitive; anti-dsDNA: specific for SLE

notes.b: Transplantation requires ABO compatibility, HLA typing (by molecular methods) of donor and recipient, and cross-matching (detecting donor-specific anti-HLA antibodies in the recipient that could cause hyperacute rejection). Rejection: hyperacute (minutes — preformed antibodies), acute (weeks–months — T-cell mediated, treatable with immunosuppression) and chronic (months–years — vascular and fibrotic). Graft-versus-host disease occurs when donor T cells attack the recipient (e.g. after bone marrow transplantation). Investigation of immunodeficiency includes full blood count and differential, immunoglobulin levels, lymphocyte subsets (CD4, CD8, CD19), complement assays (CH50) and HIV testing.
